lesson.title: Two Variables, One Picture: Building the Scatterplot
lesson.summary: Learn how to build and read a scatterplot, the essential graph for displaying the relationship between two quantitative variables, including how to correctly assign explanatory and response variables to the axes.
lesson.body:
Every graph you have studied so far describes a single quantitative variable at a time: a histogram shows the distribution of one variable, a boxplot summarizes one variable's spread. But many of the most interesting questions in statistics involve two quantitative variables at once. Does studying more hours actually raise exam scores? Does a car's age predict its resale value? Answering these questions requires a way to see two numbers per individual on the same picture, and that tool is the scatterplot.

A scatterplot plots one point for every individual in the data set, using that individual's value of one quantitative variable for the horizontal position and their value of a second quantitative variable for the vertical position. When one variable is thought to explain or predict changes in the other, the explanatory variable goes on the horizontal x-axis and the response variable goes on the vertical y-axis. This convention is not arbitrary decoration, putting the explanatory variable on the x-axis matches how later tools, like a regression line, are written and interpreted, with the response as a function of the explanatory variable.

Suppose six students report the number of hours they studied for an exam and their resulting score: (1 hour, 68), (2 hours, 72), (3 hours, 75), (4 hours, 80), (5 hours, 84), (6 hours, 90). Hours studied is the explanatory variable, since it is the one we suspect influences the outcome, so it belongs on the x-axis, exam score is the response variable and belongs on the y-axis. Plotting these six points produces a cloud that climbs steadily up and to the right: as hours studied increases, exam score tends to increase along with it.

Not every pair of quantitative variables has an obvious explanatory-response relationship. If you scatterplot a person's height and arm span, neither variable clearly causes the other, both simply grow together as part of the same body. In cases like that, the axis assignment is a matter of convenience rather than a claim about cause and effect, and you should resist the temptation to assume a scatterplot alone proves that the x-axis variable causes changes in the y-axis variable. The plot shows association, not causation.

Once the points are plotted, a scatterplot lets you evaluate four things at a glance: the overall direction of the relationship, whether it climbs or falls, the form, whether the pattern looks like a line, a curve, or no pattern at all, the strength, meaning how tightly the points cluster around that pattern, and any unusual points that stray from the rest. The next several ideas in this course, direction, form, and strength of association, are simply the vocabulary for describing what your eyes already notice when you look at a well-made scatterplot.

It is worth remembering why the scatterplot requires quantitative variables in the first place. Both axes represent a numerical scale with meaningful distances between values, which is exactly what lets you position a point precisely rather than just sorting it into a category. A categorical variable, like favorite color, has no natural numerical position on an axis, so pairing a quantitative and a categorical variable calls for a different display entirely, such as side-by-side boxplots, not a scatterplot.
